column3: Immediately precedes the command: labor brings Mary to the very palm trunk she is told to shake.
The preceding reassurance supplies water below Mary, complementing the dates provided here.
Immediate continuation: the fallen ripe dates become food alongside drink and restored composure.
Establishes Mary's pregnancy and withdrawal, the bodily and narrative setting for this provision.
Frames the miraculous birth as an easy divine act, sign, and mercy behind the commanded provision.
The announced gift of a pure son initiates the birth narrative culminating in Mary's labor and sustenance.
Pairs gestation and birth with water-stirred, growing earth, a natural analogue to the verse's labor and fruitful motion.
Water makes humbled earth stir and grow, paralleling movement that brings forth life and yield.
Describes palm clusters hanging near and fruit reaching ripeness, closely matching ripe dates made available to Mary.
Joins palms with eating their fruit at harvest, clarifying the harvest-to-nourishment movement in the focus ayah.
Links gardens of palms to abundant fruit that people eat, matching dates as divinely supplied food.
Places palm gardens beside flowing springs, combining the focus scene's fruit and nearby water provisions.
Names palms among crops brought forth by water, supplying the broader growth-to-provision pattern.
Shows palms watered by one source yet yielding differentiated fruit, a parallel agricultural sign of provision.
Calls what comes from palm fruits good provision, directly supporting the dates' nourishing role.
Its image of ripe fruit brought near complements fruit made accessible to the laboring Mary.
Recalls God's favor to Jesus and his mother, placing Mary's aid within the wider pattern of divine care for them.
Connects falling and fresh produce under divine knowledge, a distant lexical and natural-world parallel to falling ripe dates.
Gardens and springs echo the combined fruit-and-water setting surrounding the focus ayah.
A palm garden with rivers evokes the scene's palms and water, though as a skeptical demand rather than received provision.
A palm garden with streams and vulnerable children offers a distant image of family dependence on cultivated provision.
Addresses provision due to mothers during infant care, a broader social counterpart to Mary's postpartum nourishment.
A mother's grief is calmed and her eye cooled after her child's return, resonating with the consolation that follows this verse.
Uses the phrase 'coolness of the eyes' for family gift, anticipating the comfort granted to Mary after eating and drinking.
Names palms among garden fruits, a general but relevant botanical parallel.
Describes tall palms with layered fruit, a general image of the tree and yield central to the focus ayah.
Mentions cultivated fields and palms with tender clusters, a broad harvest parallel.
Lists palms among human food crops, preserving the verse's basic nourishment connection.
Brings forth water and pasture from the earth, a broad counterpart to divinely supplied sustenance.
Mary's question about bearing a son establishes the extraordinary conception whose laboring moment receives this provision.
Mary's seclusion and the messenger's arrival begin the narrative path that leads to her solitary labor by the palm.
Mary seeks refuge at the onset of the encounter, adding the vulnerability that later makes the command and provision significant.
Names the palm among the earth's fruit-bearing plants, a general botanical parallel to the date palm in the focus ayah.
Depicts fruit made near at hand, echoing the accessibility of ripe dates caused to fall for Mary.
Its cultivated garden enclosed with palms supplies a distant image of a productive palm setting.
Gardens and springs repeat the paired vegetation-and-water setting that surrounds Mary's provision.
A child is called coolness of the eye for a mother, resonating with the maternal consolation immediately following the focus ayah.
Uses the settling of the eyes and removal of grief, echoing the comfort granted to Mary after this provision.
